Seventh grade science · Unit 7.7

Earth's Resources & Human Impact

Gold, oil, copper, and water are not spread evenly across the planet. They are where they are because of Earth's deep history. You met plates and rocks in Unit 5 and energy sources in Unit 13; here we connect them to ask where resources come from, how much is left, and how people can use them wisely. Use the Unit 0: How Science Works habit of weighing evidence when you judge a solution.

Where we left off: Unit 5 explained plates and rocks, Unit 13 introduced energy resources, and Unit 7.6 showed human effects on ecosystems. You may already have learned that mantle convection moves plates. This unit connects Earth's interior and history to where resources are, and asks how people can use them wisely.

Concept 1 · Layers and heat

Earth is a heat engine

Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core. Heat from the core and from radioactive decay makes the mantle slowly convect, which moves the plates above.

Analogy

A pot of thick oatmeal

Heated from below, the oatmeal rises in the middle, spreads out, cools, and sinks at the edges. The mantle does this over millions of years, carrying plates along.

Try it

Dive into Earth

Data

Temperature with depth

Roughly 25 °C more for every kilometer down near the surface.

Concept 2 · Tectonics and ore

Plates and time decide where resources are

Many mineral resources form at plate boundaries (volcanoes bring metals up); fossil fuels formed in ancient seas and swamps; fresh water depends on climate and rock layers.

Analogy

Treasure maps

Geologists read maps of ancient seas, volcanoes, and rivers to predict where to look. Resources are clues left by Earth's past.

Concept 3 · How fast it forms

Renewable and nonrenewable resources

A renewable resource is replaced as fast as (or faster than) we use it. A nonrenewable resource takes so long to form that it is effectively gone once used.

Analogy

A bank account

Renewable: income that arrives every month. Nonrenewable: savings from your grandparents: spend it and it is gone.

Try it

Sort the resources

0 of 8 correct

Data

Years to form vs. years to use

Log scale: coal formed over ~300 million years; we use it in centuries.

Concept 4 · Using Earth

People change Earth's systems

As the human population and our resource use have grown, we have changed land, water, air, and living things: mining scars, polluted water, and rising CO₂. Good decisions weigh benefits and costs.

Analogy

A shared fridge

If every roommate takes without refilling, the fridge empties. Earth is a shared fridge with a very slow refill.

Data

Population and energy use

Billions of people. More people and more energy per person both increase the total impact.

Try it

Impacts and causes

Concept 5 · Design and decide

Evaluate solutions with criteria

Engineers and citizens compare solutions using criteria (cost, effect, safety, fairness) and trade-offs. No solution is perfect, so we weigh the evidence (Unit 0).

Analogy

Choosing a school lunch

Pizza is cheap but not healthy; salad is healthy but not filling. You pick by what matters most today.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A town wants to replace a coal power plant. Name two criteria, two possible solutions, and one trade-off for each. Which would you recommend and what evidence would you want first?

Show a model answer

Criteria: cost and emissions (also reliability). Solutions: wind plus batteries; natural gas. Wind: low emissions, higher upfront cost and needs storage. Gas: reliable and cheaper to start, but still emits CO₂ and is nonrenewable. A recommendation must cite data like cost per kWh and emissions per kWh, and the town's conditions.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

crust
Thin, rocky outer layer of Earth.
mantle
Thick, hot, slowly flowing layer.
convection
Heated material rises, cools and sinks.
renewable
Replaced naturally within a human lifetime.
nonrenewable
Takes millions of years to form.
mineral
A natural solid with a definite chemical makeup.
ore
Rock with enough metal to mine.
fossil fuel
Fuel formed from ancient organisms.
trade-off
What you give up to gain something else.
sustainable
Meeting needs without using up future resources.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $8): a pot with oatmeal or oil + food coloring (convection), a hard-boiled egg (layers model), rocks and ore samples, graph paper, a world map with plate boundaries, a recycling bin audit sheet.

  • Concept 1: Slice a hard-boiled egg and label crust, mantle, core.
  • Concept 2: Heat colored water in a clear dish to see convection.
  • Concept 3: Mark ore and oil locations on a plate map and find patterns.
  • Concept 4: Audit a week of home trash and sort into recyclable, compostable, and landfill.
  • Concept 5: Run a class debate with the decision matrix.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Earth's core is liquid so we can dig to it." We have only drilled about 12 km.
  • "Renewable means unlimited." Even wind or water has limits.
  • "Recycling solves everything." Reducing use matters more.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: when judging a solution, ask students to write the claim, the data, and the reasoning (Unit 0), and to name what they would still want to test.

After the lesson · Game

Play: Mine & Reclaim

Run a mine for ten years. Every tonne of ore earns money, but it costs land and water. Decide how much to extract and how much to put back.
